constraints: nums is a sorted array rotated between 0 and n − 1 times.

examples.explain: Rotated by zero: still fully sorted, so the minimum is first.

followUp: What if values could repeat? When nums[mid] == nums[hi] you can no longer tell which side the drop is on.
hints: A rotated sorted array is two sorted runs. The minimum is where the second run starts.
Look at nums[mid] and nums[hi]. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], where must the drop be?
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], search right of mid. Otherwise the minimum is at mid or left of it: hi = mid.

insight.mnemonic: Mid bigger than the right end? The cliff is ahead of you.
insight.oneLiner: Compare the middle with the right end: if it's bigger, the drop (and the minimum) is to the right.
insight.pattern: Binary search for the rotation point

recall.a: nums[hi] tells you whether mid..hi is sorted, even when the array isn't rotated at all. nums[mid] > nums[lo] is also true for an unrotated array, where the minimum is on the left.
recall.q: Why compare nums[mid] with nums[hi] rather than nums[lo]?

recall.a: If nums[mid] > nums[hi], mid can't be the minimum. Otherwise it might be, so it stays in the range.
recall.q: Why hi = mid but lo = mid + 1?

signals: find a pivot, break point or minimum
insight.why: Every value before the rotation point is larger than every value after it. So nums[mid] > nums[hi] means mid is still in the first run and the minimum lies right of mid; otherwise mid..hi is sorted and mid is as small as anything to its right.

oneLiner: Compare the middle with the right end: if it's bigger, the drop (and the minimum) is to the right.

pitfalls.explain: Your answer is wrong on an array that wasn't rotated (or was rotated all the way around). Comparing nums[mid] with nums[lo] can't tell 'sorted' from 'rotated'. Compare with nums[hi] instead.
pitfalls.title: Assumed the array was rotated

pitfalls.explain: The answer is the smallest *value*, nums[lo], not its position lo.
pitfalls.title: Returned the minimum's index

pitfalls.explain: When nums[mid] ≤ nums[hi], mid itself might be the minimum. Use hi = mid, not hi = mid - 1.
pitfalls.title: Skipped over the minimum

solutions.idea: Track the smallest value seen. Correct, but reads every element.
solutions.name: Linear scan

footnotes.text: Compare with the right end, not the left. nums[mid] > nums[hi] can only happen if the rotation point lies between them; otherwise mid..hi is one sorted run and nums[mid] is its smallest value.
hi = mid, not mid - 1: nums[mid] could be the minimum itself.

solutions.idea: Shrink [lo, hi] toward the rotation point: if nums[mid] > nums[hi] the drop is right of mid, otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left.
solutions.name: Binary search against the right end

statement:
An array of **distinct** integers was sorted in increasing order and then rotated: some number of elements (possibly none) were moved from the front to the back, keeping their order. For example `[2, 4, 6, 8, 9]` rotated by 2 is `[6, 8, 9, 2, 4]`.

Given the rotated array `nums`, return its smallest value in **O(log n)** time.
title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
